measures.transcript: A still-image study · read at your own pace01 / CUTTER CLEARANCEWhy the groove was neededA gear shaper strokes a disc cutter along each tooth. To finish the tooth, the cutter has to travel past the end of the face and throw its chip into open space, so the original shaft had a narrow groove just below the gear. That groove is the undercut in this story: the cutter runout and relief groove, distinct from the involute tooth-root undercut of a gear tooth.The relief gives the cutting edge room to leave the tooth face.02 / MATERIAL ATTEMPTSMaterial attemptsThree materials were tried in the grooved blank: AISI 4140 (40-45 HRC), AISI 4340 (48-50 HRC), and C300 (56-58 HRC). Each attempt was marked FAILED; these attempts are recounted by the designer.Illustrative stress concentrationAISI 4140 (40-45 HRC)FAILEDAISI 4340 (48-50 HRC)FAILEDC300 (56-58 HRC)FAILEDEarlier material attempts, as recounted by the designer.03 / A DIFFERENT PROCESSChanging the processThe failed groove design was replaced by a revised smooth blank, cut by rotary hobbing so all ten teeth formed with the approved lead-out. The revised shaft is AISI 4340 (H.T. 48-50 HRC), shown with an illustrative stress concentration rather than a certified result.Before · revised smooth blankAfter · hobbed teeth and retained sectionTwo process views · the blank and finished teeth are shown from their authored inspection angles.Illustrative stress concentrationAISI 4340 (H.T. 48-50 HRC)04 / SUPPORTS AND ASSEMBLYMoving the supportsWith the new geometry settled, the bearing and retaining-ring pair moved 2.75 millimetres into the approved final placement beside a matching housing support, and the revised assembly study returns around the operating gear train.Before · start of support relocationAfter · support pair moved +2.75 mmSame-camera study · the design moves the bearing and retaining ring together by +2.75 mm. The stills show the start of the move and its settled end.The revised assembly study

measures.transcript: A still-image study · read at your own pace01 / CUTTER CLEARANCEWhy the groove was neededA gear shaper strokes a disc cutter along each tooth. To finish the tooth, the cutter has to travel past the end of the face and throw its chip into open space, so the original shaft had a narrow groove just below the gear. That groove is the undercut in this story: the cutter runout and relief groove, distinct from the involute tooth-root undercut of a gear tooth.The relief gives the cutting edge room to leave the tooth face.02 / MATERIAL ATTEMPTSMaterial attemptsThree materials were tried in the grooved blank: AISI 4140 (40-45 HRC), AISI 4340 (48-50 HRC), and C300 (56-58 HRC). Each attempt was marked FAILED; these attempts are recounted by the designer.Illustrative stress concentrationAISI 4140 (40-45 HRC)FAILEDAISI 4340 (48-50 HRC)FAILEDC300 (56-58 HRC)FAILEDEarlier material attempts, as recounted by the designer.03 / A DIFFERENT PROCESSChanging the processThe failed groove design was replaced by a revised smooth blank, cut by rotary hobbing so all ten teeth formed with the approved lead-out. The revised shaft is AISI 4340 (H.T. 48-50 HRC), shown with an illustrative stress concentration rather than a certified result.Before · revised smooth blankAfter · hobbed teeth and retained sectionTwo process views · the blank and finished teeth are shown from their authored inspection angles.Illustrative stress concentrationAISI 4340 (H.T. 48-50 HRC)04 / SUPPORTS AND ASSEMBLYMoving the supportsWith the new geometry settled, the bearing and retaining-ring pair moved 2.75 millimetres into the approved final placement beside a matching housing support, and the revised assembly study returns around the operating gear train.Before · start of support relocationAfter · support pair moved +2.75 mmSame-camera study · the design moves the bearing and retaining ring together by +2.75 mm. The stills show the start of the move and its settled end.The revised assembly study
